```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.8, fig.height = 4.4)
```

Suppose a team has scored performances on a four-point rubric. Before the next
round, the team wants to interpret rater severity, compare two ways to spend the
same number of ratings, and pick score records to discuss in training.
`mfrmr` combines these answers in one report. This walkthrough assumes
you can run R code and have read FACETS output before.

## Load the ratings and check the calibration

The bundled synthetic data have one row per score for a `Person` from a `Rater`
on a `Criterion`. A score of 4 indicates higher performance. Scores across
criteria remain separate rows.

```{r input}
library(mfrmr)
ratings <- load_mfrmr_data("example_core")
head(ratings[c("Person", "Rater", "Criterion", "Score")], 3)

wf <- mfrm_analysis(ratings, person = "Person", facets = c("Rater", "Criterion"),
               score = "Score")
glance(wf)[c("n_obs", "n_person", "connected", "converged", "inference_status")]
```

The default rating scale model (`RSM`) uses common category steps, and the
default estimator is marginal maximum likelihood (`MML`). Check `connected`
before comparing measures across rating subsets. `inference_status = "ready"`
means the calibration passed numerical checks. Model fit and the rating design
still matter when interpreting intervals. If the status is `review_required`,
read the reason in `summary(wf)$readiness` or the report before using intervals.
For choices beyond the default, see [Choose a method for your decision](#choose-a-method-for-your-decision).

| If you start with the FACETS output | Start here in `mfrmr` |
| --- | --- |
| Table 7, measures and fit | `tidy(wf, "raters")` gives severity (`estimate`), `fair_m`, `std.error` (Model SE), `real.se` (Real SE), and Infit/Outfit. Use `tidy(wf, "persons")` for person measures. |
| Wright or variable map | `plot(wf, type = "wright")` shows the measures on the logit scale. |
| Table 4, unexpected responses | `augment(wf)` returns observed and expected scores, standardized residuals, and `.row_id` in the input. The report calls the row number `InputRow`. |
| Table 14, pairwise bias | See **Top Pairwise Bias Contrasts** in the report for a screening comparison of a rater across criteria. |

The [Table 7 manual](https://www.winsteps.com/facetman64/table7.htm),
[Table 4 manual](https://www.winsteps.com/facetman64/table4.htm), and
[Table 14 manual](https://www.winsteps.com/facetman64/table14.htm) describe the
corresponding FACETS outputs. The table above maps reading tasks. For numerical
comparisons, align the estimator, scale origin and direction, retained ratings,
and uncertainty conventions. In particular, the MML example uses EAP person
estimates by default, and the adjusted pairwise `pAdj` uses multiplicity
correction.

```{r rater-table}
tidy(wf, "raters")[c("term", "estimate", "fair_m", "infit_mnsq", "outfit_mnsq", "flag")]
```

In this example, R04 has a higher severity estimate than R02 and a lower
`Fair(M)`, the model-based average on the rubric scale under mean reference
conditions. Read severity and fit separately. Severity describes a systematic
level difference, while Infit and Outfit describe agreement with the fitted
model. An `Acceptable` flag means the workflow's screening rule did not flag
that rater. Use the original ratings and rubric to assess specific concerns.

## Compare rating plans at the same workload

For comparing people's relative standing, use the D-Study coefficient `G`.
For decisions against a fixed standard on the rubric, use absolute dependability
`Phi`, which also reflects variability due to the sampled rater or criterion
levels themselves. Both project the reproducibility of observed scores under a
specified design. FACETS separation reliability and `eap_reliability` in
`glance(wf)` refer to measures on a calibrated scale and address other questions.

```{r equal-rating-count}
plans <- tidy(wf, "d_study")
plans[plans$TotalRatingsPerPerson == 12L & plans$Rater %in% c(3L, 4L),
      c("Rater", "Criterion", "TotalRatingsPerPerson", "G", "Phi")]
```

Four raters scoring three criteria and three raters scoring four criteria both
require 12 ratings per person. Here their projected `Phi` values are about
0.831 and 0.828. The point projections are close, so feasibility and the need
to cover rubric criteria also matter. Targets such as 0.80 are examples. Choose
your own for the intended decision. A plan may assume more exchangeable
raters or criteria than are currently available. Check those assumptions and
staffing costs before adopting it.

## Review original ratings and save the report

```{r review}
rows <- augment(wf)
unexpected <- rows[rows$UnexpectedFlag,
                   c(".row_id", "Person", "Rater", "Criterion", "Observed", "Expected", "StdResidual")]
unexpected <- unexpected[order(-abs(unexpected$StdResidual)), ]
head(unexpected, 3)
ratings[head(unexpected$.row_id, 3), c("Person", "Rater", "Criterion", "Score")]

report_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".html")
render_mfrm_report(wf, format = "html", file = report_file)
rater_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".html")
invisible(render_mfrm_report(wf, rater = "R04", format = "html", file = rater_file))
```

Use the row index to look up the score and review the original response and
rubric. Large standardized residuals can prompt a data check or a second
rating. The screening flag alone gives no basis for excluding a rater.
After re-estimation, run `step_mfrm_diagnose()` again before producing
rater feedback. `augment()` can reconstruct rating-level residuals from the
current calibration when a saved diagnostic table belongs to an earlier fit.
Open the report with `utils::browseURL(report_file)` in an interactive R
session. Use `utils::browseURL(rater_file)` for the R04 feedback sheet. Supply
your own file paths to keep the HTML.

The [rater feedback guide](#tell-apart-location-bias-compression-and-halo)
explains how to read the two screens in the R04 feedback sheet.

## Use your own CSV and keep completed steps

Export one row per observed rating from your spreadsheet. Use numeric integer
scores. Leave missing ratings blank or omit their rows. The G-Study uses rows
complete for its selected identifiers and score columns and reports how many
it omits. Keep `0` for an actual score on a rubric that includes it.
Set `rating_min` and `rating_max` from the
rubric when some categories did not occur. Keep IDs with leading zeroes as
character columns when importing. This example makes a CSV with different
column names so you can run the same import and column mapping before using
your own file.

```{r csv}
csv_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
csv_example <- data.frame(Examinee = ratings$Person, Judge = ratings$Rater,
                          Dimension = ratings$Criterion, Rating = ratings$Score)
csv_example$Rating[2L] <- NA
utils::write.csv(csv_example, csv_file, row.names = FALSE, na = "")
own <- utils::read.csv(csv_file,
  colClasses = c(Examinee = "character", Judge = "character", Dimension = "character"),
  na.strings = c("", "NA"))

spec <- mfrm_workflow(own, "Examinee", c("Judge", "Dimension"), "Rating",
                      rater_facet = "Judge", rating_min = 1, rating_max = 4)
calibrated <- step_mfrm_measure(spec)
reviewed <- step_mfrm_diagnose(calibrated)
planned <- step_mfrm_gtheory(reviewed)
glance(planned)[c("n_obs", "connected", "inference_status", "phi_coef")]
```

Save the result of each step in a named object. A connected design can support
calibration while supplying too little overlap to separate G-Study variance
components. For example, keep only one criterion per examinee while the raters
still connect the groups.

```{r no-planning}
criterion_levels <- unique(own$Dimension)
assigned <- criterion_levels[(match(own$Examinee, unique(own$Examinee)) - 1L) %%
                               length(criterion_levels) + 1L]
limited <- own[own$Dimension == assigned, ]
limited_fit <- mfrm_analysis(limited, "Examinee", c("Judge", "Dimension"), "Rating",
                       rater_facet = "Judge", rating_min = 1, rating_max = 4)
glance(limited_fit)[c("connected", "inference_status")]
summary(limited_fit)$gtheory_reason
limited_report <- tempfile(fileext = ".html")
render_mfrm_report(limited_fit, format = "html", file = limited_report)
```

The warning and report give the reason planning is unavailable. The report
retains calibration and rating review. To answer the planning question,
revisit the observed overlaps and the crossed or nested design you intend to
project. The G-Study uses all declared facets by default. Use `g_facets` to
specify a subset for a different planning question or to select up to four
facets in a workflow with more than four.

## Choose a method for your decision

Start by naming the decision and the quantity it depends on. A severity
comparison, a decision about one person's score, and a recommendation to add
raters each require different evidence.

| Question | Starting analysis | What would change the analysis? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How severe are the raters overall? | RSM with MML if a common set of category steps is plausible. Read severity estimates and intervals, then review Infit/Outfit and the original ratings. | Try PCM if criteria use category transitions differently after accounting for criterion difficulty. Compare on the same ratings. |
| Do ratings from a rater or criterion distinguish performance more sharply along the ability scale? | Compare a fixed-slope model with a GPCM that frees slopes for the facet in question. Read slope intervals and predicted category curves in the relevant contexts. | Check whether the slopes are stable and change a substantive conclusion. Freeing a second slope family requires data that distinguish the two families and a reason to estimate both. |
| Does a rater systematically score one criterion higher or lower than expected? | Screen with **Top Pairwise Bias Contrasts** and inspect the original ratings. | To quantify the average location difference, use `estimate_bias(wf$fit, interaction_facets = c("Rater", "Criterion"), method = "joint")`. |
| Does a rater distinguish weaker and stronger performances within a particular domain? | Review the card's **Central tendency screen** and inspect residuals across expected score levels within that domain. | Check whether the pattern persists across performances and differs from that of other raters scoring the same performances. |
| Do residuals on different criteria move together within a rater? | Review **Criterion halo screen** and its matched-person counts. | Compare residual associations across raters scoring the same performances before attributing the pattern to halo. |
| Is a rubric subscore precise enough to report separately? | Start with domains defined by the rubric. Read [domain discrimination and dependability](#read-domain-discrimination-and-subscore-dependability) together. | Compare the precision of each subscore under the intended rating plan and examine how much the subscores vary together. |
| How many ratings are needed for relative standing or a fixed standard? | Use G-Study/D-Study for the intended observed score and allocation. Read G for relative standing and Phi for a fixed standard. | Check whether the observed design identifies the required variance components and whether the proposed allocation matches the intended use. |

### Choose the estimator and the person score separately

- **MML** integrates over an ability population. Start with the default for
  the walkthrough and check whether the population assumptions and scale are
  suitable for your data. Specify the population consistently when comparing
  models. With MML, EAP person scores shrink toward the fitted or specified
  population. Use `person_score = "WLE"` when you want weighted-likelihood
  person scoring after calibration, and record the choice.
- **CML** conditions on person totals to calibrate supported RSM and PCM
  models without specifying an ability distribution. Use it as a sensitivity
  check for facet locations if that assumption matters. Person scoring is a
  separate step.
- **JML** estimates person and facet locations jointly. It is a useful
  reference for a FACETS comparison when the scale, constraints and
  extreme-score handling match. With few ratings per person, check the
  sensitivity of person scores and rater measures. **Jeffreys-penalized JML**
  is another sensitivity check for supported RSM and PCM fits, including
  extreme scores.

For example, compare MML and CML under the same RSM and use WLE in both.

```{r estimator-sensitivity}
sensitivity <- mfrm_workflow(ratings, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion"), "Score") |>
  step_mfrm_measure(person_score = "WLE", compare_methods = "CML")
summary(sensitivity)$method_comparison[
  c("Method", "ScoreMethod", "InferenceStatus", "PersonMAD", "RaterMaxDiff")]
```

`PersonMAD` is the median absolute difference in person measures from the
primary fit. `RaterMaxDiff` is the largest absolute difference in rater
measures. Check the specific people or raters whose interpretation could
change. For example, compare the scores and uncertainty for people close to
the rubric standard. If a defensible model answers the decision and a
plausible alternative gives the same conclusion, retain the simpler model.
If the decision changes, report which assumptions matter and identify
where more rating overlap or a review of the original scores would help.

### What the recovery studies found

The simulations generated ratings from known parameters. Bias is the mean
estimate minus the truth, RMSE summarizes the size of estimation errors, and
95% interval coverage counts how often available intervals contain the
truth. Coverage measures performance across repeated samples. Also check
whether intervals were available and how wide they were.

One mfrmr 0.3.2 development study used 6 raters, 4 criteria, 5 score
categories (0 to 4), and 500 repetitions per condition (7,000 fits across
14 conditions). The usual assignment was 3 raters by 4 criteria per person
(12 ratings). The sparse assignment was 2 raters by 2 criteria (4 ratings),
with connected overlaps assigned independently of ability. The comparisons
below use 31-point MML and a fixed standard-normal ability population.
The GPCM rows use one discrimination family on the criteria, with
criterion-specific steps and slopes multiplying the full predictor.
Every fit in the study passed the numerical readiness checks.

| Scenario | Recovery result | Implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RSM with 30, 120 or 480 people and 4 or 12 ratings each | Model-SE coverage for the prespecified R6 minus R1 severity contrast (truth 1.30 logits) was 94.6% to 97.0% across the six conditions. At 120 people, reducing ratings from 12 to 4 raised person WLE RMSE from 0.341 to 0.590 logits and mean interval width from 1.31 to 2.35 logits. | Connected sparse ratings can support a calibrated rater contrast while person scores are substantially less precise. The person intervals hold the estimated calibration fixed. |
| RSM with 120 people and one rarely used rater | R6 rated just 4 people on 2 criteria each, linked through the other raters. R6 severity RMSE was 0.292 logits, with 94.2% model-SE coverage and mean width 1.13 logits. | Check exposure and interval width for that rater. The design and scale constraints contribute to the result, so 8 ratings is a description of this condition. |
| Correctly specified GPCM with 120 people | Reducing ratings from 12 to 4 raised RMSE for the C4 slope (truth 1.35) from 0.123 to 0.347 and bias from +0.017 to +0.043 on the slope scale. Log-scale model-SE intervals, transformed back to slopes, covered 96.4% and 91.6%, respectively. | Inspect slope uncertainty before using free slopes for scoring or rater feedback. |
| RSM with 120 people and 12 ratings each, with local dependence | Ratings for the same person and rater shared an omitted random effect (SD 0.6). Bias for R6 minus R1 was −0.203 logits. Coverage fell to 54.4% with model SE and was 73.0% with person-clustered sandwich SE. | Investigate dependence in the assignment and scoring process. Changing the SE leaves the point estimate and its bias in place. |

Each reported calibration interval was available in all 500 repetitions of
its condition. With that denominator the Monte Carlo standard error near 95%
coverage is about one percentage point. In the sparse GPCM condition, the C4
slope covered in 458 of 500 repetitions (91.6%, with a 95% Monte Carlo
interval of 88.8% to 93.7%). The table describes specific contrasts and
slopes under these assignments. Coverage for a new design also depends on
its overlaps, category use and model assumptions.

Two earlier development studies address different choices:

- **Estimators in a sparse RSM.** The same 1,000 datasets had 60 people,
  6 raters, 4 criteria and 8 ratings per person (2 raters by 4 criteria).
  Mean person RMSE in logits and Model-SE interval coverage were 0.535
  and 92.0% for JML with extreme-score adjustment 0.3, 0.425 and 96.1% for
  Jeffreys JML, 0.422 and 95.1% for MML/WLE with an estimated ability
  population, and 0.435 and 94.5% for CML/WLE. Coverage was averaged across
  datasets over people with usable intervals. These comparisons include the
  person scoring step, so they motivate sensitivity analysis for this
  design rather than a ranking of calibration estimators.
- **Two discrimination families.** A separate GPCM study had two levels
  each of task, rater and criterion, three score categories, and task and
  rater slopes multiplying the full predictor. With 60 people, increasing
  from 4 to 8 ratings per person reduced RMSE for a task slope with truth
  0.80 from 0.191 to 0.097. Coverage was 183/200 and 194/200, respectively,
  with all intervals available. This comparison uses a small, connected
  design with two slope families. The one-family results above concern
  criterion slopes.

### Check what kind of sparsity or bias you have

1. Count retained ratings and distinct people by rater and criterion, and
   look at their overlaps. A few shared people can link a design while
   leaving a particular contrast poorly supported. If subsets are
   disconnected, establish a substantive link through shared ratings or
   justified anchors before comparing their unanchored measures.
2. Check category counts by criterion and by the levels whose slopes you
   would estimate. Counts concentrated in one category or a missing
   category transition can leave steps and slopes weakly identified. For a
   design with little overlap or exposure, use common steps or fixed
   slopes when defensible, or collect targeted ratings. Read the readiness
   reasons and interval widths for the particular estimates you need.
3. Check whether assignment and scoring make the model's assumptions
   plausible. The sparse simulations used planned overlap and assignment
   independent of ability. If people are assigned to raters based on
   expected performance, or ratings from one person-rater pair share a
   source of dependence, assess that mechanism before using calibrated
   intervals for decisions.

## Tell apart location bias, compression, and halo

- **Location bias** changes the average observed-minus-expected score on a
  criterion after accounting for the calibration. Use **Top Pairwise Bias
  Contrasts** to screen for this pattern and a joint location contrast to
  estimate its size.
- **Compression** narrows the range of scores across performances. In the
  rater card, a negative **Central tendency screen** correlation suggests low
  expected scores may be scored up and high expected scores down. The card
  summarizes each criterion separately. To investigate one domain, use
  `augment(wf)` to inspect observed-minus-expected scores by expected score
  within that domain, then check how other raters scored the same performances.
- **Halo** can make scores on different criteria move together within the
  same performance. The card's **Criterion halo screen** gives the correlation
  of standardized residuals for a criterion pair and the number of matched
  persons. Shared features of the performance and calibration error can also
  make residuals move together. A follow-up compares within-rater residual
  associations with associations between raters scoring the same person and
  task. This comparison needs co-ratings on the same performances. Retain
  the matched counts and use the result as a screen for review.

An average gap between two criteria can change with little change in overall
fit. In a separate illustration with two rounds of 80 people
each, all four raters scored all four criteria on a four-point scale. R04
reduced the high-minus-low criterion difficulty gap from 1.80 to 0.45 logits,
while every slope stayed at one. R04's Infit MnSq was 1.05 and 0.99 in the two
rounds, both rated `Acceptable` by the report. The pairwise screen flagged the
same criterion pair in both rounds (adjusted p-values about 0.0021 and
0.00000009). The joint rater-by-criterion contrast, R04's gap minus the
other raters' mean gap, was estimated as −1.09 and −1.77 logits (truth −1.35).
Use the pairwise screen and original ratings to examine the repeated pattern,
then estimate the specified interaction if the decision requires its size.
The two rounds illustrate the diagnostic sequence, with detection probability
and within-person halo sensitivity left unestimated.

Infit and Outfit summarize residual fit, separation reliability summarizes
separation of measures, and G/Phi summarize observed-score dependability for
a specified design. The recovery figures above evaluate estimation error and
intervals. Use each diagnostic for its own question when deciding what the
data support.

The card computes residual–expected-score correlations separately within each
criterion. A raw residual correlation is not calibrated against zero: fitting
person scores can induce a negative baseline, whose magnitude depends on the
model, estimator and rating design. A fixed correction such as −1/(K−1) is
not supplied. Establish a design-matched reference before attributing an
association to halo.

## Compare models on the same ratings

Suppose you want to test whether the rubric needs criterion-specific steps,
then whether raters differ in discrimination. Fit the shared-step RSM,
criterion-step PCM, and rater-slope GPCM with the same ratings, MML estimator,
31-point integration, and fixed standard-normal ability population. Request
that population explicitly for the GPCM because its one-family default can
estimate population parameters. The slope comparison leaves criterion steps
free in both models.

```{r model-comparison}
common <- mfrm_workflow(ratings, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion"), "Score")
rsm <- step_mfrm_measure(common)
pcm <- step_mfrm_measure(common, model = "PCM", step_facet = "Criterion")
gpcm <- step_mfrm_measure(common, model = "GPCM", step_facet = "Criterion",
                          slope_facet = "Rater", gpcm_mml_identification = "fixed_standard_normal")
comparison <- anova(rsm, pcm, gpcm)
comparison$table[c("Model", "LogLik", "FreeParams", "AIC", "BIC")]
comparison$lrt
```

Read the first test as evidence about freeing the steps and the second about
freeing the slopes. A likelihood-ratio test requires compatible, nested fits.
If `lrt` is `NULL`, inspect `comparison$comparison_basis` and the warning.
Compare AIC and BIC only for compatible likelihoods. To choose a model, also
compare the result the decision depends on. For subscore reporting, compare
domain scores on the same rubric scale under the same reference rating plan.
For rater feedback, check whether the models identify the same patterns in
ratings. If you have independent ratings, compare the predictions on those
ratings as well. In a simulation with two raters per task, local dependence,
and one rater compressing one domain, adding rater slopes to criterion slopes
gave a slightly worse mean prediction on independent ratings. Its Monte Carlo
interval included both improvement and worsening.

When the question is how estimates change across estimation methods for the
same model, see
[the estimator sensitivity example](#choose-the-estimator-and-the-person-score-separately).

### Compare scores and classifications under one reference plan

For a decision on the original rubric scale, use the same people and the
same reference rating cells and weights for each model. This example compares
PCM with a GMFRM that estimates rater and criterion slopes. The reference
plan equally weights each observed rater–criterion combination.

```{r reference-plan-comparison}
dual <- fit_mfrm(ratings, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion"), "Score",
                 model = "GPCM", step_facet = "Criterion",
                 slope_facet = c("Rater", "Criterion"),
                 spec = list(slope_reference = "Criterion",
                             gpcm_mml_identification = "fixed_standard_normal"))
anova(pcm$fit, dual)$comparison_basis$lrt_status
plan <- unique(ratings[c("Rater", "Criterion")])
plan_scores <- function(fit) {
  fair_average_table(fit, reference_plan = plan)$reference_scores[c("Person", "Estimate")]
}
paired <- merge(plan_scores(pcm$fit), plan_scores(dual), by = "Person",
                suffixes = c("_pcm", "_gmfrm"))
paired <- paired[complete.cases(paired), ]
paired$Change <- paired$Estimate_gmfrm - paired$Estimate_pcm
summary(paired$Change)
with(paired, table(PCM = Estimate_pcm >= 2.5, GMFRM = Estimate_gmfrm >= 2.5))
```

The cut of 2.5 is illustrative. The scores are model expectations evaluated
at each person's primary ability estimate. Check how many people have
available scores in both models before interpreting the table. It shows
changes in the point decisions. It does not estimate error rates or
attribute the changes to slopes alone, since both models recalibrate the
other parameters.

### Score new people with a saved fit

In 0.3.2, keep the complete fit to score new people against the same
calibration. Supply the original facet columns, known rubric levels, and
observed category scores. The example gives a new ID to one rating pattern
from the bundled data to demonstrate the input format.

```{r saved-calibration-wle}
fit_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(dual, fit_file)
new_ratings <- ratings[ratings$Person == ratings$Person[1L], ]
new_ratings$Person <- "New-01"
predict(readRDS(fit_file), newdata = new_ratings, type = "wle")
```

The WLE and its SE condition on the saved calibration. Before using them for
a new cohort, check comparability of the rubric and the known levels and
review anchor displacement where applicable. This use of a saved fit
retains its original data. The 0.3.1 compact calibration file and its
new-person EAP scoring API are described in the
[archived calibration guide](https://github.com/Ryuya-dot-com/mfrmr/blob/v0.3.2/website-archive/articles/mfrmr-portable-calibration.Rmd).

## Read GMFRM discrimination and predicted responses

The **Generalized Many-Facet Rasch Model (GMFRM)** extends the
constant-discrimination many-facet Rasch model by estimating slopes, following
the terminology of [Uto and Ueno (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s41237-020-00115-7).
Use `model = "GPCM"` and specify the discrimination facets in `slope_facet`.
Choose a facet for its own category steps (many-facet GPCM) or
`step_facet = "Common"` for a shared ladder on a common rubric (many-facet RS-GPCM).

The slope plot shows each estimated slope relative to one, with intervals
when calibration supports them. With two discrimination families, read the
facets separately. The response model uses the product of the applicable
slopes. The discrimination column of FACETS Table 7 is a diagnostic obtained
after calibration. GPCM estimates slopes jointly with the other parameters.

```{r fitted-contexts, fig.height=3.9}
plot(gpcm, type = "slopes")
plot(gpcm, type = "category_curves",
     newdata = data.frame(Rater = c("R01", "R04"), Criterion = "Content"))
```

These category curves condition on the displayed rater and criterion. They
use their fitted locations, steps and all applicable slopes. A change of
context can change more than discrimination. For a GMFRM with discrimination by
two facets, specify both names in `slope_facet` and use the same `newdata`
interface. With rater and criterion slopes, the product gives every rater
the same ratio of slopes for any two criteria. The rater slope estimates
overall differences in discrimination. A rater who persistently distinguishes
performances less well in one domain can require separate domain fits and a
review of the original ratings.
For a cohort comparison, specify `dff_group` with a suitable method. The default
split likelihood test requires a supported RSM/PCM calibration. The fixed
calibration `"raju_welch"` group screen can be requested explicitly for GPCM
and answers a different question. See `?analyze_dff`.

## See what additional ratings buy

The conventional `plot(wf, type = "dstudy")` shows how a coefficient changes
as one facet count increases. The frontier view uses total ratings per person
on the horizontal axis so that allocations can be compared at equal workload.
Restrict the candidate grid to plans under consideration. Here we consider
one to five raters and two to four criteria.

```{r frontier}
planning <- step_mfrm_gtheory(common, target_g = 0.80, target_phi = 0.85,
                             d_study_grid = expand.grid(Rater = 1:5, Criterion = 2:4))
plot(planning, type = "dstudy_frontier")
```

Points show allocations. The step line rises whenever a higher point
projection becomes achievable within the rating count. A label shows the
allocation with the highest projection at the smallest count meeting the
target in that panel. `tidy(planning, "d_study")` provides the full comparison.
Treat small gaps as point estimates, and check staffing and rubric coverage
before deciding. D-Study counts for nested facets are per parent level.

## Read domain discrimination and subscore dependability

Suppose a rubric reports two subscores, the mean of Content and Organization
and the mean of Language and Accuracy. Define the domains from the rubric
before looking at the slopes. In the bundled `example_core` data, each
`Person`–`Rater` pair has one score on each of the four criteria. Keep those
scores in separate rows for the GMFRM.

```{r domain-slopes}
domains <- list(ContentOrganization = c("Content", "Organization"),
                LanguageAccuracy = c("Language", "Accuracy"))

fit_criterion_slopes <- function(data, points = 31L) {
  fit_mfrm(data, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion"), "Score",
           model = "GPCM", method = "MML", step_facet = "Common",
           slope_facet = "Criterion",
           spec = list(gpcm_mml_identification = "unconstrained_slopes",
                       slope_type = "ability_only",
                       noncenter_facet = c("Person", "Criterion")),
           control = list(mml_integration = "adaptive", quad_points = points))
}

pooled <- fit_criterion_slopes(ratings)
by_domain <- lapply(domains, function(criteria) {
  fit_criterion_slopes(ratings[ratings$Criterion %in% criteria, ])
})
fits <- c(list(Pooled = pooled), by_domain)
vapply(fits, function(fit) summary(fit)$readiness$status, character(1))
lapply(fits, function(fit) fit$slopes[c("Level", "Estimate", "ModelSE")])
```

All three models use a fixed standard-normal ability distribution and allow
criterion slopes to vary on that scale. The pooled fit estimates one ability
for the full rubric. Each domain fit estimates ability using only the criteria
assigned to it. If a calibration needs review, read the reasons in
`summary(fit)$readiness` for that fit before interpreting its slopes.
Interpret slopes in relation to the ability used in that fit.
Separate fits have separate ability scales. Report a difference in subscores
on the original rubric scale under a common reference rating plan when that
difference is the quantity of interest.

When a slope would change the decision, check sensitivity to the integration
rule as well as the calibration status. For example, refit with more adaptive
quadrature points and inspect how much the estimates change. One simulation
dataset returned successful calibration status under both rules, yet the
mean domain slope was 1.32 with 65 fixed points and 1.57 with 31 adaptive
points. An independent integration check supported the adaptive result
for that dataset.

```{r domain-quadrature}
pooled_finer <- fit_criterion_slopes(ratings, points = 55L)
summary(pooled_finer)$readiness
merge(pooled$slopes[c("Level", "Estimate")],
      pooled_finer$slopes[c("Level", "Estimate")],
      by = "Level", suffixes = c("_31_points", "_55_points"))
max(abs(fitted(pooled, type = "probs") - fitted(pooled_finer, type = "probs")))
```

For the multivariate G-Study, compute the two observed subscores for each
person–rater pair. The example uses a 60% and 40% composite. For other data,
use your rubric's scoring rule for missing criteria. Here `rowMeans()`
requires both scores in a domain, and the G-Study reports any incomplete
rows it omits. Include the task in the pairing and G-Study design if the
same person and rater contribute multiple tasks.

```{r multivariate, fig.height=3.4, fig.alt="Generalizability and dependability of the two subscores and their weighted composite at the observed rating counts."}
wide <- stats::reshape(ratings[c("Person", "Rater", "Criterion", "Score")],
                       idvar = c("Person", "Rater"), timevar = "Criterion",
                       direction = "wide")
for (domain in names(domains)) {
  wide[[domain]] <- rowMeans(wide[paste0("Score.", domains[[domain]])])
}
multivariate <- step_mfrm_gtheory(wf, g_data = wide, g_facets = "Rater",
                                 g_scores = names(domains), g_weights = c(.6, .4))
tables <- summary(multivariate)$report_tables
tables[["Subscore generalizability"]][c("Score", "G", "Phi")]
components <- tables[["Subscore variance-covariance components"]]
person_components <- components[components$Component == "Person", ]
person_components[c("ScoreA", "ScoreB", "Estimate", "CovarianceStatus")]
plot(multivariate, type = "gstudy")
```

Read `G` for relative standing and `Phi` for a fixed standard under the
declared design. The composite uses the covariance within each component, so
its coefficients need not equal the weighted mean of the subscore
coefficients. The person component describes how universe scores vary
together. If its covariance matrix is valid and the two person variances
are positive, use `stats::cov2cor(multivariate$gtheory$vcov_components[["Person"]])`
for the person-component correlation. In these ratings the reported matrix
is invalid, so the correlation is unavailable. The subscore coefficients
are available and address the precision of each subscore. The full report
shows both results through `render_mfrm_report(multivariate)`.

In a simulation where a speaking rubric had a distinct pronunciation and
fluency domain, its mean slope was about two-thirds of the content domain's
slope on the pooled scale. The mean slopes were similar when estimated
within their own domains, and the pronunciation and fluency `G` was about
0.92 in the no-halo conditions. When the simulation instead lowered the
true slopes on a shared ability, both the within-domain slopes and `G`
were lower. A small pooled slope warrants review of domain precision and
the intended construct before removing or downweighting a criterion.
These patterns do not supply cutoffs for diagnosing multidimensionality.

For planning the number of raters, `plot(multivariate, type = "dstudy_frontier")`
projects dependability for the declared composite. For a particular subscore,
run `step_mfrm_gtheory()` for that score on the same complete rating rows.

## References

- Brennan, R. L. (2001). *Generalizability Theory*. Springer. doi:10.1007/978-1-4757-3456-0
- Eckes, T. (2015). *Introduction to Many-Facet Rasch Measurement*. Peter Lang. doi:10.1007/978-3-662-45601-5
- Linacre, J. M. (1989). *Many-Facet Rasch Measurement*. MESA Press.
